d.title: A handler captures the one piece of evidence 1.2 argued for
d.caption: The `prompts` argument of `on_llm_start` is **the resolved prompt as it was actually sent** — which is the evidence 1.2 argued is the only thing that tells you what a chain really did. Templates, partials and placeholders are all gone by that point; what arrives is the flat message list. A handler is how you capture it in production, where you cannot put a `print` between two steps of a pipe.

nodes.label: And you cannot print inside a pipe
nodes.sub: which is why a handler exists

d.title: Seven things a callback sees, one it sees conditionally, one nothing can
d.caption: The token row is the one that shapes 4.4: **a callback sees characters for free and tokens only if the provider returns them — and only after the call.** Which is useless for control, so 4.4 counts locally instead. And the last row is worth stating rather than leaving implied: **no instrumentation anywhere answers why the model chose what it chose**, so every lesson in this module is about observing behaviour rather than explaining it.

cells.text: only if reported, and only after

d.title: Per-invocation, which is correct and is also the bug people write
d.caption: Handlers go in `config={"callbacks": [...]}`, so **they are per-invocation.** That is the right design — two concurrent requests should be recorded separately. It is also exactly where the mistake lives: **a handler that accumulates state across invocations is a bug that only appears under load**, because a single-request test cannot distinguish a per-call counter from a shared one.

nodes.label: And is wrong only under load
nodes.sub: which is when you find it

d.title: 86% of the run is one model call, which decides where optimisation goes
d.caption: Total 59.9 ms, model call 51.5 ms, **everything else 8.4 ms.** Which is the same finding the GenAI observability module reached from the other direction: the framework overhead everyone argues about is the small term, and **work that does not change the model call, the prompt or the number of calls is work on 14% of the request.** Self time is what makes that visible — a span's own cost with its children subtracted.

d.title: Four things to attach, and the one teams miss
d.caption: **The request-id row is the one teams miss most often.** A trace store and an application log are two separate systems, and without a shared identifier, correlating *"the user who complained at 14:32"* with a specific run is manual and **usually impossible at volume**. It costs one entry in metadata, and it is only cheap before you need it.

items.label: run_name
items.sub: a readable span name instead of RunnableSequence

items.label: a request id in metadata
items.sub: ties a trace to your own logs - the row teams miss

d.title: Readable helps one person; queryable answers the first question
d.caption: A `run_name` makes a span **readable** — you are not staring at forty rows called `RunnableSequence` matching step indices by hand. Tags and metadata make a trace **queryable**: *show me the failures for this tenant, this version, this experiment arm.* **Readable helps one person debugging one run. Queryable is what lets you ask whether a problem is general**, which is almost always the first question — and only the second degrades as traffic grows.

nodes.label: run_name: readable
nodes.sub: a name instead of an index

nodes.label: And only readable degrades with traffic

d.title: Hit rate is free to compute and points the wrong way
d.caption: Ten queries about the same thing: **exact match gets 2 hits and a 0.5 similarity threshold gets 8.** So lowering the threshold quadruples the hit rate, which looks like a straightforward win and is the number every dashboard carries. It is also **the number that rewards exactly the behaviour §03 shows is dangerous** — because a looser threshold increases hits by joining queries that are not the same question.

d.title: Three pairs that are different questions with high word overlap
d.caption: **"reset my password" and "reset my username" score 0.50.** So does *cancel my order* against *cancel my account* — a pair where serving one answer for the other is a support incident. The measurement that actually matters is therefore **wrong-hit rate**, which needs a labelled sample of query pairs and a judgement about which differences change the answer. **That is real work, which is why hit rate is what most teams track.**

d.title: Four things that must never be cached
d.caption: The first row is the one with a security consequence rather than a quality one: **a cached answer for user A served to user B.** The third is the one that is easy to forget because the cache key looks right — the question is identical and **the index may have changed underneath it**, so a RAG answer cached yesterday is an answer about yesterday's corpus with today's confidence.

items.label: Anything personalised
items.sub: a cached answer for user A served to user B

d.title: The provider's count is fine for accounting and useless for control
d.caption: 4.1 established that a callback sees provider token counts **only if reported, and only after the call.** That is adequate for accounting and useless for control: **enforcing a budget, deciding how many chunks fit, or refusing an over-long request all require the number before the request is made.** Which is the whole reason to count locally — not accuracy, but timing.

nodes.label: The reason is timing, not accuracy
nodes.sub: which is the thing to see

d.title: The question the system exists to answer is 3% of the input
d.caption: **Retrieved context is 89% of the input**, which is the usual shape for RAG and the reason 7.3 spends a lesson on budgeting it. The system prompt is 8%. And the user's question — **the thing the whole system exists to answer — is 3%.** Which reframes where to look when a prompt is too long: trimming instructions and rephrasing the question are rounding errors, and the chunk count is the only term that matters.

d.title: The point is not the number, it is that it is computed
d.caption: A system that counts before sending can **refuse an over-long request with a useful message, drop the lowest-scoring chunks deliberately, or summarise instead.** A system that does not count **discovers the limit as a provider error**, which 3.5 showed is unrecoverable mid-conversation — and arrives on exactly the long conversations you least want to drop. The budget is a code path rather than a hope, and that is the whole difference.

d.title: max_bucket_size is the burst allowance after idle; the rate is what you settle to
d.caption: Five acquires, three bucket sizes. **A bucket of 1 is a strict metronome** — one free, then four waits, 0.81 s. A bucket of 5 absorbs the whole burst and costs **0.00 s**, then throttles afterwards. So the two parameters answer different questions: **the rate is your sustained throughput and the bucket is how much of a spike you can pass through without smoothing it.**

d.title: Five differences between handling 429s and not causing them
d.caption: Read down the right-hand column: **the request is never made, so there is nothing to bill, nothing to retry and no storm to have.** The second row is the one people do not expect — **a rejected request may still be billed**, depending on the provider and where the rejection happened. And the last two rows are the compounding pair: failures correlated across a burst are what turns a brief limit into an outage, and a client-side limiter removes the correlation rather than the symptom.

cells.text: adds load to a busy provider

d.title: Four workers at five per second is twenty at the provider
d.caption: `InMemoryRateLimiter` holds its bucket **in memory**, so the limit is per process and not per service. **Four workers each limited to five requests per second is twenty at the provider** — and the number to configure is the provider limit divided by the worker count, **which means it has to change when you scale.** A limiter that was correct at two workers is four times too permissive at eight, silently, with no code change involved.

d.title: Four wrong orderings, and what each one silently does
d.caption: The last row is the one that costs most and is hardest to see: **cache hits consume rate-limit tokens**, so the cache stops being free exactly when traffic is high enough for it to matter. **The cache belongs outermost for the same reason it exists: a hit should cost nothing** — not a model call, not a token from the limiter, not a retry budget. And the first row is 2.6's measured inversion: fallback inside retry gives the primary **one** attempt.

items.label: Fallback inside retry
items.sub: the primary gets ONE attempt (2.6, measured)

items.label: Rate limit inside retry
items.sub: a three-retry burst takes three times as long as it needs

items.label: Cache inside the retry
items.sub: a cached answer is not used on the retry path

d.title: The fallback is for when retrying is not enough, not for the first hiccup
d.caption: The composition is worth **asserting on rather than assuming**, because the inverted version does not raise — it works, and costs more. **A fallback that fires on every transient failure shows up as an unexplained bill from the secondary provider rather than as an error**, which is the hardest kind of misconfiguration to find: nothing is broken, the answers are fine, and the invoice is wrong in a way that looks like traffic growth.

nodes.label: Assert on it
nodes.sub: the inverted version does not raise

nodes.label: Inverted: fallback on the first hiccup

d.title: What each mechanism is not for
d.caption: Stated as negatives because that is where the misuse lives. **A rate limiter controls requests, not cost** — one request with a 100k-token prompt passes a limiter that would reject ten small ones. **A fallback masking a primary you have not measured** means you never learn the primary's real failure rate, so the fallback becomes load-bearing by accident. And the last row applies to all five: **none of them is a substitute for knowing why something fails.**

items.label: Fallback
items.sub: masking a primary you have not measured

items.label: All of them
items.sub: a substitute for knowing why something fails

d.title: What a guardrail can and cannot do
d.caption: The model receives **a single sequence of text.** There is no field that says *this part is data, treat it as inert* — the system message is a convention with training behind it, **not an enforced boundary.** So instruction and data are distinguishable only by the model's judgement, which is exactly what an attacker targets. The third row is the exception worth separating: **a `ValidationError` from a schema is enforced by your code rather than requested of the model**, which is 1.5's distinction and the one genuine guarantee here.

items.label: Raise the cost of an attack
Constrain output shape

d.title: Five defences that make damage impossible rather than unlikely
d.caption: Every row is structural, and the difference from a guardrail is the verb: these **make something impossible** rather than detecting an attempt. **An agent that cannot delete cannot be talked into deleting**, however the request is phrased — which is the only kind of defence that survives a phrasing nobody has seen. The last row is the cheapest and the most often skipped: **nothing to extract is a complete defence against extraction.**

items.label: Least privilege on tools
items.sub: an agent that cannot delete cannot be talked into it

items.sub: a document never fetched cannot be leaked (1.6)

items.sub: an interrupt before the tool runs (9.7)

d.title: A secret in a prompt is in six places you did not choose
d.caption: It is **in the prompt, in the provider's logs, in your trace store, in the context window of every subsequent turn, and extractable by any successful injection.** The correct arrangement is that **the tool holds the credential and the model can only call the tool** — which also makes the permission boundary a real one rather than an instruction, because the model never possesses the thing it would need to exceed its permissions.

nodes.label: The tool holds the credential
nodes.sub: the model only calls the tool

d.title: The machinery is deterministic once the token generation is
d.caption: This is why the course runs on a scripted model at all, and **the same technique is what makes a test suite possible.** Everything around the model — prompt rendering, trimming, parsing, routing, retries, the message list — is ordinary deterministic code. Replace the one non-deterministic component with a script and **all of it becomes assertable**, which is a far larger share of a real system than people expect.

nodes.label: The model is the only non-determinism
Which is most of a real system

d.title: The assertion that catches the most is about the prompt, not the answer
d.caption: Three assertions on what the model **received** rather than what it returned: the message count, the system message surviving unchanged, and the question actually interpolated. That last one is 1.3's silent failure caught — **an unapplied partial sends the literal `{tone}` and produces a plausible answer**, so asserting on the answer passes and asserting on the prompt does not. **Testing the input is where the cheap bugs are.**

d.title: Three kinds of test, and only one of them has a threshold
d.caption: **Deterministic** tests assert exact behaviour against a scripted model and either pass or fail — ordinary unit tests, and most of what this module can be tested with. **Property** tests assert something true for every input, which is how you check an invariant like *the system message survives trimming* without enumerating cases. **Evaluation** is the only one with a threshold and a trend, and therefore the only one that can be flaky by design.
